newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Portraits of major political players in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Portraits of major political players in Russia.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's admission to hospital with the first signs of pneumonia has prompted speculation that other political leaders could start jostling for position in his absence.
The following are brief portraits of key players on Russia's political arena.

ALEXANDER LEBED, 46. Has no official post after Yeltsin sacked him last October as Russia's security chief for his open presidential ambitions. The outspoken Lebed finished a strong third in the first round of the presidential election on June 16 and his popularity grew after he signed a peace deal to end fighting in rebel Chechnya on August 31. Since his sacking, Lebed has kept a relatively low profile but has started trying to build a political movement. He urged Yeltsin to quit soon after the president was taken to hospital on Wednesday.

VIKTOR CHERNOMYRDIN, 58. Prime Minister. Stolid, pro-reform leader who is Russia's number two under the constitution. Has presented an image of calm, and kept his options open in the power struggle last year while Yeltsin was ill. Has a good relationship with Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais and both want Yeltsin to stay in office as long as possible because Chernomyrdin is not thought likely to beat Lebed in an early presidential election.

YURI LUZHKOV, 60. Moscow Mayor. Won landslide re-election last June. Says he has no immediate presidential ambitions but has kept high public profile recently, taking a strong nationalist stance. Has good relationship with Yeltsin and smooth relations with Chernomyrdin, but history of feuding with Chubais.

GENNADY ZYUGANOV, 52. Communist Party leader. Was second to Yeltsin in presidential election runoff last July but says he could win if the president stepped down now. Has recently forged wider alliance with other leftist and nationalist groups to strengthen the left's bid for power. His presidential ambitions are hampered by limited access to mass media, lack of charisma and few financial resources. Russian media have speculated over whether he and Lebed might join forces.

ANATOLY CHUBAIS, 41. Head of presidential administration. Unlikely presidential challenger, at least for some years, but his post as Yeltsin's chief-of-staff gives him huge influence and makes him a potential kingmaker. Regarded as an excellent organiser and a master of behind-the-scenes intrigues. Has long alliance with Chernomyrdin and is fierce critic of Zyuganov.

TATYANA DYACHENKO, 36. Yeltsin's daughter. She has no formal Kremlin post but helped organise her father's successful re-election campaign. Kremlin officials publicly play down the significance of her role but some independent analysts suggest she has a have big influence on Yeltsin. Independent Russian political analysts suggest she and Chubais share similar views in the power struggle. The analysts suggest she still has a powerful role behind the scenes but the extent of her influence remains unclear. Some media reports say she may get an official Kremlin position shortly.
